title: How People Learn & Barriers to Learning
whatItIs: DVSA guidance says pupils learn in different ways and at different speeds. Instructors must spot barriers to learning and help the learner find ways round them.
keyFacts: Pupils prefer different approaches: some learn actively, others want time to reflect first.
Learners who aren't engaged or just receive information cope less well when driving alone.
Barriers can include delivery methods, times, location, lack of facilities or of special needs support.
Plan for literacy, numeracy and language issues, and for physical or cognitive disabilities.
Cultural factors matter, e.g. eye contact, or a belief that contradicting the teacher is 'bad manners'.

items.title: Eye contact
items.text: Use good eye contact, where this is culturally acceptable.

items.title: Consistent language
items.text: Use the same, consistent language throughout.

items.title: Manageable pieces
items.text: Break things down into manageable pieces.

items.title: Visual aids
items.text: Use pictures and other visual aids to back up your words.

a.label: Learns actively
points: May solve a problem straight away in discussion

b.label: Reflects first
points: May need to go away and think it over
May need pointing to reading or other inputs

onTheTest.question: Which of these does the national standard list as a possible barrier to learning?
onTheTest.why: Element 6.3.1 lists barriers such as delivery methods, times, location, lack of special needs support and lack of facilities.

onTheTest.question: A pupil can't answer a problem on the spot. What does DVSA guidance suggest?
options: Allow time to reflect, or suggest reading
Always give the answer and move on
Treat them as not ready for test
onTheTest.why: Examiner guidance 3.24: some pupils need to reflect or be pointed to reading; pushing for answers on the spot may be unproductive.

traps: Hours of tuition don't show ability: different people learn in different ways at different speeds.
You can't force learning: the pupil sets the pace, so spot when they stop learning.
Your own assumptions about groups in society can affect how well you teach.
If a learner's needs exceed your competence, transfer them to an appropriate colleague.
